kp.k: Katyal reports bespoke AI support for Supreme Court preparation
kp.d: The article reports that Milbank partner Neal Katyal used a bespoke Harvey AI system to prepare for November oral argument against President Donald Trump’s tariffs. According to the reported TED Talk, the system was trained on 25 years of justices’ oral-argument questions and eventual opinions. Katyal claimed it predicted many questions, sometimes almost verbatim; this is his account of the tool’s performance, not a reported independent evaluation.
qs: he said during a [TED Talk](https://www.ted.com/talks/neal_kumar_katyal_what_really_won_the_trillion_dollar_supreme_court_case) released Thursday that he “won” using a “bespoke AI system” trained on 25 years of justices’ questions during oral argument and their eventual opinions.
The system was built by Harvey AI, which “predicted many of the questions the justices asked—sometimes almost word for word,” Katyal said in an X post promoting the TED Talk.

kp.k: Critics contest attributing litigation success to AI-assisted preparation
kp.d: The article reports online criticism of Katyal’s account, noting that several elite law firms and dozens of amicus briefs contributed to the case. Daniel Epps questioned the portrayal of AI and personal coaching as decisive. The Supreme Court held the tariffs illegal in a 6-3 decision in February, but the reported dispute concerns what contributed to that outcome, rather than whether the AI system was used.
qs: Social media posts and online columns published by the National Review and the Volokh Conspiracy pushed back against Katyal’s comments about the case, which involved work by several elite law firms and included dozens of amicus briefs, Bloomberg Law reports.

“The notion that it’s Katyal’s preparation with his mindfulness coach and AI that was the key difference maker, I just think people think that was a little preposterous,” Daniel Epps, a professor at the Washington University School of Law in St. Louis, told Bloomberg Law.

In February, the Supreme Court [held](https://www.abajournal.com/columns/article/chemerinsky-six-takeaways-from-the-supreme-courts-tariffs-decision) in a 6-3 decision in [Learning Resources Inc. v. Trump](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/24-1287_4gcj.pdf) that the tariffs Trump imposed are illegal.

kp.k: Prediction tools offer potential value, with uncertain outcome influence
kp.d: Mitu Gulati viewed the TED Talk as demonstrating the potential value of AI prediction tools and reinforcing Katyal’s reputation for Supreme Court litigation. He nevertheless doubted that oral argument changed any justice’s vote, while framing the possibility of changing a vote as a reason clients pay for such advocacy. These are Gulati’s assessments, not measured findings about AI’s effect on judicial decisions.
qs: Mitu Gulati, a University of Virginia law professor who studies the Supreme Court, noted some benefits to Katyal’s TED Talk, telling Bloomberg Law it showed the potential value of AI prediction tools.
He also said it reinforced Katyal’s reputation as a “go-to lawyer” for Supreme Court litigation.
“Everybody reads everything and it’s hard to imagine oral argument changed anybody’s vote,” Gulati told Bloomberg Law. “That said, if you can change a vote, that’s why you pay the guy.”

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Katyal claims bespoke AI helped prepare his Supreme Court advocacy by anticipating justices’ questions; its contribution to winning the case is disputed.
pts.d: Amanda Robert reports Katyal’s account that a bespoke Harvey AI system helped him prepare for the tariffs argument and predicted questions with sometimes near-verbatim accuracy. The article reports his characterization that he won using the system, rather than establishing AI as the cause of the outcome. Mitu Gulati identifies potential value in AI prediction tools, while Daniel Epps challenges the suggestion that Katyal’s AI-assisted preparation and coaching were the decisive difference. Gulati also doubts that oral argument changed votes. These are claims about assistance to an experienced advocate, not replacement of lawyers or autonomous litigation.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is a single practitioner’s case account and expert commentary, not a measured evaluation of prediction accuracy or causal impact.
pts.d: Katyal’s TED Talk and promotional X post supply the account of successful question prediction. The reported system was trained on 25 years of justices’ oral-argument questions and eventual opinions; this describes its training basis, not an independently tested performance result. The Supreme Court’s 6–3 ruling against the tariffs supplies outcome context, but the article provides no comparison or other evidence isolating AI’s contribution. Robert also reports several elite firms’ involvement and dozens of amicus briefs, while Epps and Gulati offer expert qualifications to the victory narrative.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The reported use concerns preparation for a November argument followed by a February decision; no broader adoption or performance forecast is supplied.
pts.d: The 2026 article describes a retrospective use in one Supreme Court tariffs case. It dates the argument to November, the decision to February, and the TED Talk’s release to Thursday. The benefit is tied to a bespoke system and an experienced Supreme Court advocate. Gulati’s qualification separates useful preparation from the much harder claim that oral advocacy changed a justice’s vote.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate application is elite Supreme Court advocacy, with potential preparation benefits for counsel and perceived value for clients.
pts.d: Katyal, a Milbank partner, is the reported user; Harvey AI built the system. The claimed benefit is better anticipation of judicial questioning during high-stakes oral argument. Gulati also says the talk reinforced Katyal’s reputation as a specialist Supreme Court lawyer and connects a lawyer’s potential ability to change a vote with why clients pay for representation. The article does not claim market-wide changes in staffing, fees, access to justice, or lawyer displacement.
